title: Open items after the wave 0 decisions
intro: R1, R2, R3 and D7 are applied. Tests this round closed the sandbox questions: cat, python3 and the Read tool are blocked; local and remote MCP servers (the real Tavily server, key from TAVILY_API_KEY) work with the sandbox on; allowedDomains lets a listed domain through; a sandbox that cannot apply fails the command. Five calls remain.

decisions.title: Sandbox for gate commands and cmd tasks
decisions.ref: Module 8 run_gates; module 9 CommandAdapter; decision D7
decisions.context: D7 turns on Claude Code's sandbox, which covers only Claude workers. A gate such as `make build` and any `cmd` task runs through CommandAdapter as a plain subprocess, with the engine's full access to your files. Tested on macOS: Anthropic's standalone `srt` (@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime 0.0.83) denied a read, refused a write outside the worktree, allowed one inside it, and ran a piped command.

options.name: Run every cmd task and gate command under srt, with the same read and write rules as the workers
pros: Same boundary for workers and commands, built by Anthropic
Tested: read denied, outside write refused, in-worktree write allowed
The repo's own scripts cannot read the factory home
cons: One more dependency: an npm package, pinned at 0.0.83, that the kit must install and doctor must check
Linux is not tested, and the macOS path rests on the deprecated sandbox-exec
Build tools that write caches outside the worktree fail until listed (see Q2)

options.name: Leave cmd tasks and gates unsandboxed and state it as residual risk
pros: No new dependency or code
No cache-path problems for builds
cons: A gate command runs with full user access, so D7 protects workers but not the repo's own scripts
A planted script in the repo can read the factory home

options.name: Write the factory's own sandbox-exec and bubblewrap wrapper for commands
pros: The factory owns the profile
cons: Two code paths to build and test
Duplicates what srt already does
This was the option D7 declined

decisions.why: srt is the same mechanism Claude uses, it passed the same canary, and it closes the one path D7 left open.

decisions.title: Where build caches go under the write boundary
decisions.context: Tested with the sandbox on: a write to ~/.npm failed with Operation not permitted, while a write inside the worktree worked. npm, Maven and Gradle write caches under your home folder, so a worker or gate that installs or builds fails unless the cache path is writable. Tested names: npm_config_cache works and npm_cache does nothing.

options.name: Point each tool's cache at a folder under the task's work/ folder (npm_config_cache, MAVEN_OPTS, GRADLE_USER_HOME), set by the adapter
pros: The write boundary stays exactly two paths
Nothing a worker writes persists outside the run
No shared cache for one run to poison
cons: Each task downloads dependencies again, so builds are slower
Each language profile in 17A needs its cache variable named
Needs network access to the package registry for every task

options.name: Add one factory cache folder, such as $FACTORY_HOME/cache, to allowWrite and point every tool at it
pros: Dependencies download once per machine
Faster builds
cons: A third writable path, shared across runs and repos
One run can write a bad package that a later run installs
Breaks the 'writes only to the worktree and task folder' rule that D7 states

options.name: Add ~/.npm, ~/.m2 and ~/.gradle to allowWrite
pros: Tools work unchanged
cons: A worker can write into your own tool caches
Breaks the D7 rule
Cache poisoning reaches your own builds

decisions.why: It keeps D7's two-path rule intact, and speed can be bought back later with a read-only shared cache.

decisions.title: String commands in gates and join_cmd
decisions.ref: Section 18 GateSpec.cmd; module 5 YAML; module 7 join_cmd
decisions.context: Section 18 freezes GateSpec.cmd as list[str] and module 3 requires argument lists with no shell. Seven commands in module 5's YAML and one in module 4 are strings (`cmd: "make build"`), and module 7 writes `join_cmd: "npm install --package-lock-only"`. That is nine, and none uses shell syntax such as a pipe or &&.

options.name: Rewrite the nine examples as argument lists and make a string an error at load
pros: Matches module 3's no-shell rule and the frozen type
No parsing rule to document or get wrong
The schema check catches the mistake before a run
cons: Slightly noisier YAML: [make, build] for make build
Repos copying the examples must use lists

options.name: Accept a string and split it into words with shlex at load; still no shell
pros: The short form in the examples stays valid
Still no shell is used
cons: A hidden rule: quotes and spaces in a path split in surprising ways
The frozen type gains a second input form to test

options.name: A string runs through the shell, a list does not
pros: Pipes and && work in a gate
cons: Contradicts module 3 and breaks Windows later
Opens injection through request text that reaches a command

decisions.why: Nine examples are cheap to fix now, and a list keeps one meaning for the frozen type.

decisions.title: RunSpec shape
decisions.ref: Section 18; module 5 TaskSpec and plugin manifest
decisions.context: TaskSpec has `run: RunSpec | None` and the readiness review lists RunSpec as undefined without proposing a shape. Module 5 shows two forms in the plugin manifest: `run: {script: <path>, args: [...]}` and `run: {python: <module:function>}`.

options.name: RunSpec has script: str | None, python: str | None, args: list[str]; exactly one of script and python is set
pros: Matches both forms module 5 already shows
Small, and checkable by the schema
The os: rule from module 5 applies to script only
cons: A third kind of task, such as a container, needs a new field

options.name: RunSpec is a tagged union with a kind field: script, python
pros: Adding a kind later is a new variant, not a new field
cons: Changes the YAML in module 5 to add kind: script
More ceremony for two kinds

decisions.why: It freezes exactly what the spec already writes and changes no example.

decisions.title: Linux and OAuth login: when to test
decisions.ref: Decision D6 and D7; module 9 isolation
decisions.context: Neither is tested. This machine is macOS with a gateway token. Linux needs bubblewrap, and Claude Code names it in the binary. An OAuth login needs a machine that has one. Both change whether D7 holds, and wave 0 does not need either.

options.name: Test both before the phase 1a pilot run; the doctor canary fails on any machine where it does not pass
pros: Wave 0 starts now
doctor already proves the boundary per machine, so an untested machine cannot silently run workers
The pilot is the first run on the owner's real setup
cons: Linux support is claimed in D6 but unproven until then
A surprise could change the module 9 text late

options.name: Test both now, before wave 0
pros: No claim goes into code unproven
cons: Blocks wave 0 on machines and logins this session does not have
Wave 0 touches neither

options.name: Declare phase 1a macOS only and move Linux to 1b
pros: Claims only what was tested
cons: Reopens D6, which stands
Needs your sign-off on a scope change

decisions.why: doctor makes an untested machine fail closed, so waiting costs nothing.
